content: Automated and quantitative results are expected to make interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) more objective compared to the tuberculin skin test (TST). However, performing IGRA tests requires a well-equipped laboratory, expensive equipment, and specialized training, which may present logistical challenges. Research Priorities Further research aimed at improving the accuracy of IGRAs is strongly encouraged. Such studies should adhere to robust study designs, including the use of representative populations, prospective follow-up, and proper blinding procedures. It is also recommended that proof-of-principle studies be followed by well-designed evaluation and demonstration studies to assess their impact on patients. These studies should be implemented prospectively and provide evidence to support their findings. WHO Guidelines on Tuberculosis Testing The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis (TB) testing, including recommendations for the use of TST and IGRAs. These guidelines emphasize the following: 1. Conditional Recommendation for TB Antigen-Based Skin Tests (TBSTs): TBSTs may be used to test for TB infection, but the evidence supporting this recommendation is of very low certainty. 2. Use of TST or IGRAs: Either TST or IGRAs can be used to test for TB infection. This is a strong recommendation, but the certainty of the evidence remains very low. 3. Limitations of IGRAs in Lowand Middle-Income Countries: IGRAs should not replace TST in lowand middle-income countries for diagnosing latent TB infection in children, adolescents, or individuals living with HIV. They should also not be used for the diagnostic work-up of active TB in these populations. This recommendation supersedes earlier guidance from 2011. 4. Screening in Healthcare Workers: IGRAs should not be used in healthcare worker screening programs in lowand middle-income countries. 5. Outbreak Investigations and Contact Screening: IGRAs should not replace TST for screening latent TB infection in adult and pediatric contacts or during outbreak investigations in lowand middle-income countries. 6. Risk Identification for Active TB: Neither IGRAs nor TST should be used in lowand middle-income countries to identify individuals at risk of developing active TB. 7. Diagnosis of Pulmonary or Extrapulmonary TB: IGRAs and TST should not be used for diagnosing pulmonary or extrapulmonary TB or for the diagnostic work-up of adults suspected of active TB in lowand middle-income countries, including those living with HIV. Guideline Development Process The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) followed a structured process to develop these recommendations. This included drafting PICO (Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome) questions, identifying patient-important outcomes, and conducting evidence reviews. Meetings were held either in person or virtually, depending on circumstances such as the COVID-19 pandemic. Decisions were made by consensus or, if necessary, by voting. Concerns and differing opinions were documented and included in the final evidence-to-decision tables. Conflict of Interest Assessment All GDG and External Review Group (ERG) members were required to submit declarations of interest (DOI) forms, which were reviewed by the WHO steering committee. Financial and non-financial interests were evaluated to identify potential conflicts of interest. Significant conflicts, such as intellectual bias or financial interests exceeding $5,000, were managed appropriately. Developers of diagnostic assays were excluded from the policy development process to avoid conflicts of interest. Summary of Changes in Recommendations The 2022 update to the WHO guidelines introduced several changes compared to earlier versions from 2011 and 2020. These include the conditional recommendation for TB antigen-based skin tests and the strong recommendation against using IGRAs in certain low-resource settings for diagnosing latent or active TB. Conclusion The WHO guidelines aim to provide evidence-based recommendations for TB testing while addressing logistical, economic, and ethical considerations.
